755.t: Eve of the An Lushan Rebellion
755.d: The Tang in the winter of Tianbao 14 (755), before An Lushan's rising. On the frontiers stood ten military governorships and pacification commissions: Anxi, Beiting, Hexi, Longyou, Shuofang, Hedong, Fanyang, Pinglu, Jiannan and the Five Commands of Lingnan; in the interior, investigation commissioners still supervised the prefectures and counties in fifteen circuits. An Lushan alone held the three fanzhen of Fanyang, Pinglu and Hedong, with nearly 200,000 troops. All around, Tibet, Nanzhao, the Uyghurs, Balhae, the Khitans and the Xi lay in wait.

756.t: Two capitals fall · Accession at Lingwu
756.d: In the 1st month of Tianbao 15 (756) An Lushan proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan at Luoyang. Yan Gaoqing and Yan Zhenqing rose in Hebei for the court, but Changshan fell in the 1st month and Pingyuan was abandoned in the 10th, and Hebei passed back to Yan. In the 6th month Geshu Han was defeated at Lingbao and Tong Pass was lost; Emperor Xuanzong abandoned Chang'an and fled west, at Mawei Station the imperial guards killed Yang Guozhong and forced Yang Guifei to hang herself, and Xuanzong went on into Shu. In the 7th month Crown Prince Li Heng took the throne at Lingwu (Emperor Suzong) and changed the reign title to Zhide. The Yan army held the two capitals and most of Henan, while Zhang Xun at Yongqiu, Lu Jiong at Nanyang and Xue Yuan at Yingchuan barred its way south to the Jiang–Huai region. Nanzhao took advantage of the turmoil to seize Xizhou.

757.t: Two capitals recovered · Shi Siming surrenders to the Tang
757.d: In the 1st month of Zhide 2 (757) An Qingxu murdered his father and took his place. Li Guangbi held Taiyuan, and Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan defended Suiyang to the death for ten months, shielding the Jiang–Huai region. In the 9th month Li Chu, Prince of Guangping, and Guo Ziyi, with Uyghur troops, routed the Yan army at Xiangji Temple and recovered Chang'an; in the 10th month they won again at Xindian and recovered Luoyang, and An Qingxu fled north to Yecheng (Xiangzhou), still holding seven commanderies and more than sixty towns. In the 12th month Shi Siming surrendered to the Tang with Fanyang and twelve other commanderies and was made Prince of Guiyi and military governor of Fanyang, though he kept his army in his own hands. Emperor Suzong returned to Chang'an, and Emperor Xuanzong came back from Shu. With the Tang western armies drawn east, Tibet began to eat into Longyou.

759.t: Rout at Yecheng · Shi Siming retakes Luoyang
759.d: In the 6th month of Qianyuan 1 (758) Shi Siming rebelled again; in the 9th month Emperor Suzong ordered nine military governors, Guo Ziyi and Li Guangbi among them, to besiege Yecheng together, with no supreme commander and with the eunuch Yu Chao'en as army supervisor. In the 3rd month of Qianyuan 2 (759) Shi Siming came south to the city's relief; as the armies met north of the Anyang River a great wind sprang up, and the 600,000-strong Tang army scattered. Shi Siming then killed An Qingxu, proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan at Fanyang in the 4th month, and in the 9th month crossed the Yellow River and took Bianzhou and Luoyang again; Li Guangbi abandoned Luoyang and fell back to the three cities of Heyang, where he held the Yan army at bay. The Tang kept Guanzhong, Shanguo, eastern Henan and the Jiang–Huai region.

763.t: An Lushan Rebellion ends · Tibet enters Chang'an
763.d: In Shangyuan 2 (761) Shi Siming was killed by his son Shi Chaoyi. In the 10th month of Baoying 1 (762) the Tang, with Li Kuo, Prince of Yong, as supreme commander and with Uyghur troops, recovered Luoyang again, and Shi Chaoyi fled north; in the 1st month of Guangde 1 (763), cornered, he hanged himself, and the An Lushan Rebellion was over after more than seven years. Eager to end the fighting, the court divided Lulong, Chengde, Weibo and Xiangwei among the surrendered rebel generals Li Huaixian, Li Baochen, Tian Chengsi and Xue Song, and Hebei's autonomy began; Hou Xiyi of Pinglu led his troops across the sea and moved his seat to Qingzhou. Taking advantage of the empty garrisons of Hexi and Longyou, Tibet seized every prefecture of Longyou, and in the 10th month broke into Chang'an and set up Li Chenghong, Prince of Guangwu, as emperor; Emperor Daizong fled to Shanzhou, and fifteen days later Guo Ziyi recovered the capital.

765.t: Hebei autonomy · Hexi and Longyou lost
765.d: In Guangde 2 (764) Tibet took Liangzhou; the military governor of Hexi fell back on Ganzhou, Suzhou, Guazhou and Shazhou, and from then on Anxi and Beiting were cut off from the Central Plains. Pugu Huai'en, the great general of Shuofang, was driven into rebellion and twice led over 200,000 Uyghur, Tibetan, Tangut and other troops in invasions; in the 9th month of Yongtai 1 (765) Huai'en died of illness in his camp, and Guo Ziyi rode alone into the Uyghur camp and made a treaty with them, and together they struck the Tibetans at Xiyuan near Lingtai. In the same year the Ziqing army mutinied, and Li Zhengji drove out Hou Xiyi and set himself up. By now military governors and surveillance commissioners had been set up everywhere in the interior, and fanzhen covered the empire.

777.t: Ziqing's fifteen prefectures · Weibo takes Xiangwei
777.d: In Dali 8 (773) Xue Song, military governor of Xiangwei, died; in Dali 10 (775) Tian Chengsi of Weibo stirred up a mutiny at Xiangzhou and seized the four prefectures of Xiangzhou, Weizhou, Mingzhou and Cizhou. Emperor Daizong ordered the fanzhen to attack him, but the campaign was called off without result: Tian Chengsi kept Xiangzhou and Weizhou, while Xingzhou, Mingzhou and Cizhou went to Li Baozhen of Zelu and were joined with it as the Zhaoyi Jun. In Dali 11 (776) Li Lingyao, acting military governor of Biansong, revolted and was put down by the combined forces of several fanzhen; Li Zhengji of Ziqing took the chance to seize the five prefectures of Caozhou, Puzhou, Xuzhou, Yanzhou and Yunzhou, which with Dezhou, taken from Weibo, gave him fifteen prefectures in all. He moved his seat to Yunzhou and became the strongest fanzhen in Henan, while Bianzhou, Songzhou and their neighbors went to Li Mian of the Yongping Jun. Tibet took Ganzhou and Suzhou (766) and then Guazhou (776), leaving Hexi only Shazhou.

782.t: The four fanzhen proclaim themselves kings
782.d: In Jianzhong 2 (781) Li Baochen of Chengde died; his son Li Weiyue was refused the succession and joined Tian Yue of Weibo, Li Zhengji of Ziqing and Liang Chongyi of Shannan East Circuit in defying the court. That year Li Zhengji died and his son Li Na succeeded him; Emperor Dezong had Li Xilie of Huaixi crush Liang Chongyi, and Li Wei, prefect of Xuzhou, came over to the court with his prefecture. In the 1st month of 782 Ma Sui and others routed Tian Yue at the Huan River and besieged Weizhou; Li Weiyue was killed by his officer Wang Wujun, and the court split Chengde into three fanzhen: Hengji (Wang Wujun), Shenzhao (Kang Rizhi) and Yi-Ding-Cang (Zhang Xiaozhong, called the Yiwu Jun). Resentful at his meager reward, Wang Wujun joined Zhu Tao of Lulong to relieve Weibo, and in the 6th month they routed the Tang army at Qieshan; in the 11th month Zhu Tao proclaimed himself King of Ji, Wang Wujun King of Zhao, Tian Yue King of Wei and Li Na King of Qi, and the "four fanzhen" formed an alliance; in the 12th month Li Xilie styled himself Supreme Commander of All Under Heaven and King of Jianxing. Tibet took Yizhou.

784.d: In the 10th month of Jianzhong 4 (783) the Jingyuan troops mutinied as they passed through Chang'an and set up Zhu Ci as emperor (as Qin, later renamed Han), and Emperor Dezong fled to Fengtian, where he was besieged for over a month; in the 12th month Li Xilie took Bianzhou. In the 1st month of Xingyuan 1 (784) Dezong issued an edict of self-reproach; Wang Wujun, Tian Yue and Li Na gave up their royal titles and submitted, but Li Xilie proclaimed himself emperor at Bianzhou with the dynastic name Great Chu. In the 2nd month Li Huaiguang of Shuofang also rebelled and held Hezhong, and Dezong fled again to Liangzhou, which he raised to Xingyuan Fu. In the 5th month Li Sheng recovered Chang'an, and in the 7th month Dezong returned to the capital; Zhu Tao, besieging Beizhou, was defeated by Wang Wujun and Li Baozhen and fell back to Youzhou. Tibet had taken all of Hexi except the isolated city of Shazhou. (The map shows spring 784, when Chang'an, Hezhong and Bianzhou were still held by Zhu Ci, Li Huaiguang and Li Xilie.)

787.d: In Xingyuan 1 (784) Zhu Ci fled in defeat and was killed by his own men; in Zhenyuan 1 (785) Ma Sui and Hun Jian pacified Hezhong and Li Huaiguang killed himself; in Zhenyuan 2 (786) Li Xilie was poisoned by his officer Chen Xianqi, and Huaixi submitted for a time before Wu Shaocheng seized power. The Jianzhong rebellions were over, though the fanzhen of Hebei, Ziqing and Huaixi still passed from father to son. The Tibetan chief minister Shang Jiezan raided Jingzhou, Longzhou, Binzhou and Ningzhou year after year and took Shazhou in 786 (787 by another account), and with it the last of Hexi; in 787, when Tang and Tibet met at Pingliang to swear a treaty, Tibetan troops lying in ambush seized the Tang party, and the Tang envoy Hun Jian barely escaped with his life. The chief minister Li Mi set out the strategy of "making peace with the Uyghurs to the north, opening ties with Nanzhao to the south and allying with the Arabs to the west" to contain Tibet.

794.d: In Zhenyuan 4 (788) Princess Xian'an was married to the Uyghur khagan, and the Uyghurs soon changed the Chinese characters of their name from Huihe to Huihu. Allied with the Karluks and the White-Robed Turks, Tibet took Beiting in 790; the Uyghur relief army was routed, and Yang Xigu, military governor of Beiting, fell back to Xizhou and was later killed by the Uyghurs. Around 792 Xizhou fell too, leaving the garrisons of Anxi isolated beyond the frontier and cut off from news of the Central Plains. Wei Gao, military governor of Xichuan, won Nanzhao over: in 794 Yimouxun, King of Nanzhao, swore a covenant with the Tang envoy Cui Zuoshi on the Diancang Mountains and returned to the Tang against Tibet, and promptly routed the Tibetans at Shenchuan, taking sixteen towns, Tieqiao City among them. In the interior Zhang Jianfeng held Xuzhou (788), and Wu Shaocheng of Huaixi and Li Na and his son of Ziqing each held their own ground.

805.t: Tibet at its height · Fanzhen everywhere
805.d: In the later Zhenyuan years the garrisons of Anxi fell one after another: Khotan and Kashgar went to Tibet, while Kucha, Karasahr and Beiting were taken by the Uyghurs, and Tang rule in the Western Regions came to an end; Tibetan power reached the Long Mountains in the east and was at its height. Wei Gao, military governor of Xichuan, allied with Nanzhao and defeated Tibet again and again, fighting a great battle around Weizhou in 801. In the interior the three Hebei fanzhen, Li Shigu of Ziqing (twelve prefectures) and Wu Shaocheng of Huaixi took power without the court's sanction, and Emperor Dezong simply tolerated them. In 805 Emperor Shunzong came to the throne; Wang Shuwen, Wang Pi and others launched the Yongzhen Reform, which failed within half a year, and Emperor Xianzong succeeded.

817.t: Caizhou taken on a snowy night
817.d: On coming to the throne Emperor Xianzong resolved to curb the fanzhen: in Yuanhe 1 (806) he put down Liu Pi of Xichuan and Yang Huilin of Xiasui, and in Yuanhe 2 (807) Li Qi of Zhexi; his campaign against Wang Chengzong of Chengde in Yuanhe 4–5 achieved nothing. In Yuanhe 7 (812) Tian Ji'an of Weibo died, and Tian Hongzheng submitted to the court with Weibo's six prefectures. In Yuanhe 9 (814) Wu Shaoyang of Huaixi died and his son Wu Yuanji set himself up; the court sent troops against him, and Li Shidao of Ziqing came to his aid by having the chief minister Wu Yuanheng assassinated and the Heyin transport depot burned. In Yuanhe 12 (817) Pei Du went to the front to direct the campaign himself, and in the 10th month Li Su took Caizhou by surprise on a snowy night and captured Wu Yuanji; Huaixi was pacified, and its three prefectures of Shenzhou, Guangzhou and Caizhou were divided among neighboring fanzhen. Chengde, Lulong and Ziqing still defied the court.

820.d: In Yuanhe 13 (818) Wang Chengzong of Chengde gave up the two prefectures of Dezhou and Dizhou and sent his son to court as a hostage; in Yuanhe 14 (819) Li Shidao of Ziqing was killed by his officer Liu Wu, and Emperor Xianzong divided his twelve prefectures into the three fanzhen of Tianping, Pinglu and Yanhai. "For nearly sixty years since the Guangde era the fanzhen had defied the court in more than thirty prefectures of Henan and Hebei, appointing their own officials and paying no tribute or taxes; now all of them obeyed the court's commands." In the 1st month of that year Emperor Xianzong was murdered by eunuchs, and Emperor Muzong came to the throne. In the north the Uyghurs and Tibet faced each other north and south of the Tian Shan.

822.t: Hebei revolts again · Treaty of Changqing
822.d: In Changqing 1 (821) Liu Zong of Lulong handed his lands over to the court, gave up his office and became a monk; the court sent Zhang Hongjing to Youzhou and transferred Tian Hongzheng to Chengde, and mishandled both: in the 7th month the Youzhou army imprisoned Zhang Hongjing and set up Zhu Kerong, and the Chengde army killed Tian Hongzheng and made Wang Tingcou acting military governor. The court's punitive campaign achieved nothing, and in the 1st month of 822 Tian Bu, military governor of Weibo, killed himself and Shi Xiancheng took over. The three Hebei fanzhen were autonomous once more, and the Tang never recovered them. Tang and Tibet swore treaties at Chang'an (821) and Rasa (822), fixing the border and ending the fighting; in 823 the Tang–Tibet Treaty Pillar was set up in front of the Jokhang in Lhasa, and the frontier stayed largely quiet for the next twenty years.

844.d: In Kaicheng 5 (840) the Yenisei Kyrgyz sacked the Uyghur khagan's camp and the Uyghur Khaganate collapsed; its people went over to the Karluks or moved west to the Tian Shan and Hexi, while Wujie Khagan led the remnants south to the Tiande and Zhenwu frontier, where the Tang general Shi Xiong routed them at Mount Shahu in Huichang 3 (843). In Huichang 2 (842) the Tibetan tsenpo Langdarma was assassinated and the royal house split; frontier commanders such as Lun Kongre and Shang Bibi fought one another, and the Tibetan Empire broke up into tribes. In 843 Liu Congjian, military governor of Zhaoyi, died, and his nephew Liu Zhen defied the court; the chief minister Li Deyu directed the campaign against him, and Zelu was pacified in the 8th month of 844. The three Hebei fanzhen remained hereditary and independent.

851.t: Zhang Yichao returns to allegiance · Hehuang recovered
851.d: The Tibetan tribes fought among themselves, leaving Hexi and Longyou empty. In Dazhong 2 (848) Zhang Yichao of Shazhou rose and drove out the Tibetans, recovering Guazhou and Shazhou; in Dazhong 3 (849) the Tang recovered the three prefectures of Qinzhou, Yuanzhou and Anle Zhou and the Seven Passes; in Dazhong 5 (851) Zhang Yichao sent his elder brother Zhang Yitan to court with the maps and household registers of eleven prefectures, and the Tang set up the Guiyi Jun with Zhang Yichao as military governor. One branch of the Uyghurs who had moved west held Xizhou, Beiting and the Karasahr region, and Khotan too threw off Tibetan rule. In Huichang 5 (845) Emperor Wuzong suppressed Buddhism; the next year Emperor Xuanzong came to the throne and Buddhism revived. The three Hebei fanzhen remained hereditary and independent.

863.d: In Dazhong 13 (859) Emperor Xuanzong died and Emperor Yizong came to the throne; Shilong, King of Nanzhao, proclaimed himself emperor, renamed his state Dali (Great Rites), broke with the Tang and raided Annan and Xizhou again and again. In Zhedong Qiu Fu rose in revolt (859–860), gathering as many as 30,000 followers before Wang Shi put him down. In Xiantong 2 (861) Zhang Yichao took Liangzhou, and the Hexi Corridor was open again. In the 1st month of 863 Nanzhao took Giao Châu; Cai Xi, Protector-General of Annan, died in battle, the Tang army fell back to Haimen, and Nanzhao held Annan for three years.

869.d: In Xiantong 7 (866) Gao Pian defeated the Nanzhao army and recovered Giao Châu, built the citadel of Đại La and reorganized Annan as the Jinghai Jun; in the same year the Uyghur leader Pugu Jun took Xizhou and Beiting and founded the Kingdom of Qocho. In Xiantong 9 (868) Xuzhou soldiers garrisoning Guizhou marched home north without orders, choosing Pang Xun as their leader; they took Xuzhou in the 10th month and held Xuzhou, Suzhou, Haozhou and other prefectures, cutting the Jiang–Huai canal route. The court sent Kang Chengxun against them with troops borrowed from the Shatuo leader Zhuye Chixin (Li Guochang), and the rising was crushed in the 9th month of 869. At the end of the year Shilong of Nanzhao threw his whole army into an invasion of Xichuan, and the next year he besieged Chengdu. (The map shows the situation when Pang Xun held Xuzhou, Suzhou and Haozhou.)

881.d: In Xiantong 11 (870) Nanzhao besieged Chengdu but was driven off by Tang troops, and from then on its strength declined. In Qianfu 1–2 (874–875) Wang Xianzhi and Huang Chao rose in Henan and Shandong and fought their way through the Jiang–Huai region; after Wang Xianzhi was defeated and killed in 878, Huang Chao led his followers south into Zhejiang and Fujian, took Guangzhou in 879 and turned back north, crossed the Huai in 880, took Luoyang in the 11th month, and in the 12th month broke through Tong Pass and entered Chang'an, where he took the throne as emperor with the dynastic name Great Qi; Emperor Xizong fled to Chengdu. Shi Pu of Xuzhou, Qin Zongquan of Caizhou and others set themselves up amid the chaos; Li Keyong and his father of the Shatuo were defeated by a Tang army in 880 and fled north to the Tatars. In the northwest the Guiyi Jun and the Kingdom of Qocho stood side by side.

886.t: Qin Zongquan proclaims himself emperor · Xizong flees again
886.d: In Zhonghe 3 (883) Li Keyong and his Shatuo army routed Huang Chao at Liangtianpo and recovered Chang'an in the 4th month; Huang Chao went east and besieged Chenzhou for nearly three hundred days, was crushed by Zhu Quanzhong and Li Keyong in 884, and died in the 6th month at Langhu Valley near Mount Tai. That same year Zhu Quanzhong tried and failed to murder Li Keyong at the Shangyuan Post Station in Bianzhou, and the two became sworn enemies. Qin Zongquan of Caizhou, who had gone over to Huang Chao, carried on the rebellion and proclaimed himself emperor in 885; his officers raided in all directions and held Luoyang, Heyang, Ruzhou, Zhengzhou, Xuzhou, Shanzhou, Guozhou, Xiangzhou, Dengzhou and other places, massacring wherever they went. Emperor Xizong returned to the capital in 885, but when the eunuch Tian Lingzi quarreled with Wang Chongrong of Hezhong over the salt lakes, Wang Chongrong and Li Keyong of Hedong defeated the Binning and Fengxiang troops on Tian's side and closed on the capital, and Xizong fled again to Fengxiang and Xingyuan; in 886 Zhu Mei of Binning changed sides, set up Li Yun, Prince of Xiang, as emperor in Chang'an, and was killed at the end of the year.

895.d: In Guangqi 3 (887) Zhu Quanzhong routed Qin Zongquan at Bianxiao Village outside Bianzhou; the next year Qin Zongquan was seized by his own officers, Henan gradually passed to Zhu Quanzhong, and he went on to swallow Shi Pu of Xuzhou (893). Li Keyong held Hedong and Zhaoyi and fought Zhu Quanzhong year after year; Li Maozhen held Fengxiang and Shannan West Circuit and joined Wang Xingyu of Binning and Han Jian of Huazhou in holding the court in their grip, until Li Keyong came south in 895 and destroyed Wang Xingyu. Wang Jian took Xichuan in 891, and Yang Xingmi destroyed Sun Ru in 892 and held Huainan; Qian Liu held Hangzhou, Dong Chang proclaimed himself emperor at Yuezhou in 895 (the state of Great Yue Luoping), Wang Chao held Fujian, and Ma Yin and Liu Jianfeng took Hunan. Weibo, Chengde and Liu Rengong of Youzhou wavered between Zhu and Li.

903.t: Siege of Fengxiang · Zhu Quanzhong controls the emperor
903.d: In Qianning 4 (897) Zhu Quanzhong swallowed Zhu Xuan of Tianping and Zhu Jin of Taining, and in the same year marched south against Yang Xingmi but was badly defeated at Qingkou, after which he could never cross the Huai. He then took Xingzhou, Mingzhou and Cizhou in the north (898), forced Weibo, Chengde and Yiwu to submit (900), and in 901 took Wang Ke's Hezhong and Zelu, pressing west on Guanzhong. The eunuch Han Quanhui carried Emperor Zhaozong off to Li Maozhen at Fengxiang; Zhu Quanzhong besieged Fengxiang for over a year, and in the 1st month of 903 Li Maozhen killed the eunuchs and handed over the emperor. Zhu Quanzhong brought the emperor back to Chang'an in his own hands and put all the eunuchs to death; in the same year Wang Shifan of Pinglu was defeated and surrendered to Zhu. Wang Jian seized the chance to take Li Maozhen's Shannan West Circuit and Jingnan's three prefectures of Kuizhou, Zhongzhou and Wanzhou; Li Keyong was shut up in Hedong, and Liu Rengong of Youzhou annexed Cangzhou and Jingzhou. Yang Xingmi was invested as Prince of Wu, Qian Liu held both Zhexi and Zhedong, and Ma Yin took the Gui Command.

907.t: Fall of Tang · Five Dynasties begin
907.d: In Tianyou 1 (904) Zhu Quanzhong forced Emperor Zhaozong to move the capital to Luoyang and pulled down the palaces of Chang'an; that same year he had Zhaozong murdered and set up Emperor Ai. In 905 at Baima Station he killed more than thirty court officials and threw their bodies into the Yellow River. In the 4th month of Tianyou 4 (907) Zhu Quanzhong usurped the Tang throne, changed his name to Zhu Huang and founded the state of Liang (Later Liang) with its capital at Kaifeng; the Tang came to an end. Li Keyong of Hedong, Li Maozhen of Fengxiang and Yang Wo of Huainan (Wu) still used the Tang reign title "Tianyou" and opposed Liang; in the 9th month of the same year Wang Jian of Xichuan proclaimed himself emperor at Chengdu (Former Shu). Qian Liu was invested as Prince of Wuyue and Ma Yin as Prince of Chu; Wang Shenzhi held Fujian (invested as Prince of Min in 909), Liu Yin held Guangzhou, Liu Shouguang of Youzhou imprisoned his father and took his place, and Wang Rong of Zhenzhou and Wang Chuzhi of Dingzhou each went their own way. In the same year the Khitan leader Yelü Abaoji took the title of khagan.

915.t: Jin destroys Yan · Weibo goes over to Jin
915.d: In Kaiping 2 (908) Li Keyong died and his son Li Cunxu succeeded him as Prince of Jin, at once routing the Liang army at its double-walled siege camp before Luzhou. In Qianhua 1 (911), at the Battle of Baixiang, the combined armies of Jin and Zhao crushed the Liang army, and Wang Rong, Prince of Zhao, and Wang Chuzhi, Prince of Beiping, attached themselves to Jin. Liu Shouguang proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan in 911; in 913 the Jin general Zhou Dewei took Youzhou, and Yan fell. In 912 Zhu Wen was murdered by his son Zhu Yougui, and the next year Zhu Youzhen (the last Liang emperor) came to the throne. In Zhenming 1 (915) Liang split Weibo into two fanzhen; the Weizhou army mutinied and surrendered Weizhou, Bozhou, Beizhou and other prefectures to Jin, Liang lost most of Hebei, and the two armies faced each other across the Yellow River. In the south Wu destroyed Wei Quanfeng of Fuzhou (909), Chu annexed Langzhou and Lizhou, and Liu Yan of Qinghai took the Rong and Yong Commands.

923.d: In Zhenming 2 (916) Jin took all the prefectures of Hebei; that same year Yelü Abaoji of the Khitan proclaimed himself emperor and campaigned west against the tribes of the Hetao; in 917 Lu Wenjin, commander at Xinzhou, went over to the Khitans, and the Khitans besieged Youzhou for two hundred days. In 918 Liang and Jin fought a great battle at Huliupo in which both sides suffered heavily. Former Shu took advantage of Qi's weakness to seize Qinzhou, Chengzhou, Jiezhou and other prefectures. In 921 Zhang Wenli of Zhenzhou murdered Wang Rong, Prince of Zhao, and in 922 the Jin army took Zhenzhou, bringing Chengde into Jin. In the 4th month of Tongguang 1 (923) Li Cunxu proclaimed himself emperor at Weizhou with the dynastic name Tang (Later Tang); in the 10th month he struck from Yunzhou at the Liang capital, Daliang, in a lightning march, the last Liang emperor took his own life, and Later Liang fell; Li Maozhen sent a memorial acknowledging himself a subject. In the south Liu Yan proclaimed himself emperor in 917 (Southern Han), Wu took Qianzhou (918), and Wang Geon replaced Taebong with Goryeo in 918.

926.t: Former Shu falls · Khitan destroys Balhae
926.d: In Tongguang 2 (924) Li Maozhen, Prince of Qi, died; his lands had already acknowledged Later Tang as overlord. In 925 Emperor Zhuangzong sent Li Jiji, Prince of Wei, and Guo Chongtao against Shu and destroyed Former Shu in seventy days, appointing Meng Zhixiang to Xichuan and Dong Zhang to Dongchuan. In 926 the army at Yedu mutinied, and in the 4th month, in the Xingjiao Gate incident at Luoyang, Zhuangzong was killed and Li Siyuan took the throne (Emperor Mingzong). In the same year Yelü Abaoji of the Khitan campaigned east, took Huhan City and destroyed Balhae, turning it into the state of Dongdan with Crown Prince Yelü Bei as Renhuang Wang (King of Men); Abaoji died of illness on his way home. In the south Wu, Wuyue, Min, Chu, Southern Han and Jingnan stood side by side.

934.d: In Tiancheng 3 (928) Wang Du of Yiwu rebelled in league with the Khitans, and the next year Dingzhou fell; in 930 Yelü Bei, King of Dongdan, fled by sea to Later Tang. From 930 Meng Zhixiang of Xichuan and Dong Zhang of Dongchuan together defied the court; in 932 Xichuan and Dongchuan turned on each other, Dong Zhang was defeated at Jizong Bridge and died, and Meng Zhixiang held both Xichuan and Dongchuan; in 933 Later Tang attacked Li Yichao at Xiazhou without success, and from then on the Dingnan Jun held Yinzhou and Xiazhou as its own. After Emperor Mingzong's death, Meng Zhixiang proclaimed himself emperor at Chengdu in the 1st month of 934 with the dynastic name Shu (Later Shu); in the 2nd month Li Congke, Prince of Lu, rose at Fengxiang, and in the 4th month he entered Luoyang and seized the throne; and Zhang Qianzhao of Shannan West Circuit and others surrendered Xingyuan and neighboring prefectures to Shu.

938.t: Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun pass to Khitan
938.d: In Qingtai 3 (936) Shi Jingtang, military governor of Hedong, rebelled at Jinyang; when the Later Tang army besieged Jinyang, Yelü Deguang of the Khitan came to his aid in person with a great army, routed the Tang army and invested Shi Jingtang as emperor (Later Jin); in the intercalary 11th month Shi Jingtang entered Luoyang, and the last Later Tang emperor burned himself to death. Calling himself the Khitans' "son emperor", Shi Jingtang ceded the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun to the Khitans (formally handed over in 938) and paid 300,000 bolts of silk a year; from then on the Central Plains lost the barrier of the Great Wall in the north. In 938 he moved the capital to Kaifeng. In the same period Xu Zhigao (Li Bian) replaced Wu with Southern Tang in 937, Duan Siping destroyed Dayining and founded the Dali Kingdom (937), Wang Geon of Goryeo united the Korean peninsula (936), and in Giao Châu Ngô Quyền crushed Southern Han at the Bạch Đằng River in 938; Vietnam moved toward independence.

947.d: The Later Jin emperor Shi Chonggui (Emperor Chu) called himself the Khitans' grandson but not their subject, which led to war; in 946 Du Chongwei surrendered to the Khitans with an army of 100,000 at the Zhongdu Bridge, and in the 1st month of 947 Yelü Deguang entered Kaifeng and Later Jin fell; in the 2nd month he changed the dynastic name to Great Liao. Liao troops went out in all directions plundering for supplies ("gathering grass and grain"), resistance broke out across the Central Plains, and in the 3rd month Yelü Deguang went back north; he died on the way in the 4th month. Liu Zhiyuan, military governor of Hedong, proclaimed himself emperor at Taiyuan in the 2nd month (Later Han) and entered Kaifeng in the 6th month. In the south, Southern Tang destroyed Min in 945, Li Renda of Fuzhou went over to Wuyue, and the three prefectures of Qinzhou, Chengzhou and Jiezhou surrendered to Later Shu.

951.t: Later Zhou founded · Southern Tang conquers Chu
951.d: In 950 Emperor Yin of Later Han murdered his senior ministers; Guo Wei rose at Yedu and entered Kaifeng, and in the 1st month of 951 proclaimed himself emperor and founded Later Zhou. Liu Zhiyuan's younger brother Liu Chong proclaimed himself emperor at Taiyuan (Northern Han) and became a dependent of Liao. In the south the Ma brothers of Chu fell out, and in 951 Southern Tang took the chance to destroy Chu; Southern Han seized Chu's prefectures in Lingnan along with Chenzhou and Lianzhou; Liu Congxiao of Quanzhou held the two prefectures of Quanzhou and Zhangzhou (the Qingyuan Jun). Later Shu had already gained the four prefectures of Qinzhou, Fengzhou, Chengzhou and Jiezhou.

955.t: Battle of Gaoping · Zhou takes Qinzhou and Fengzhou
955.d: In Guangshun 2 (952) Liu Yan and Wang Kui, former officers of the Ma family of Hunan, rose and drove out Southern Tang, regaining Hunan, and Later Zhou appointed them to the Wuping Jun. In Xiande 1 (954) Emperor Taizu of Later Zhou died and Chai Rong took the throne (Emperor Shizong); Liu Chong of Northern Han came south with Liao troops, and Shizong took the field in person, crushed Northern Han and Liao at Gaoping and pressed on to besiege Taiyuan without taking it, then went home and reorganized the palace army. In 955 Shizong sent Wang Jing and Xiang Xun west against Later Shu, taking the four prefectures of Qinzhou, Fengzhou, Chengzhou and Jiezhou in the 11th month; he also issued edicts restricting Buddhism and put the finances in order, and in the winter sent Li Gu south against Southern Tang's Huainan.

959.t: Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou campaigns south and north
959.d: From Xiande 3 to 5 (956–958) Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou campaigned three times against Southern Tang; in 957 he routed the Southern Tang relief army at Mount Zijin and took Shouzhou, and in 958 Southern Tang ceded its fourteen prefectures north of the Yangtze (Yangzhou, Taizhou, Chuzhou, Hezhou, Shouzhou, Haozhou, Sizhou, Chuzhou, Guangzhou, Haizhou, Shuzhou, Qizhou, Huangzhou and Luzhou); the two states took the Yangtze as their border, and Li Jing gave up the title of emperor for "ruler of the state". In Xiande 6 (959) Shizong campaigned north against Liao and in forty-two days recovered the two prefectures of Yingzhou and Mozhou and the three passes of Waqiao, Yijin and Yukou, but soon died of illness. After Wang Kui's death in Hunan, Zhou Xingfeng held the Wuping Jun.

963.d: In the 1st month of Xiande 7 (960) Zhao Kuangyin seized power in the Chenqiao mutiny and replaced Zhou with Song, keeping Kaifeng as the capital; in the same year he put down the revolts of Li Yun at Luzhou and Li Chongjin at Yangzhou, and the next year he relieved his generals of their commands "over a cup of wine" and adopted the strategy of "south first, then north". In 962 Zhou Xingfeng of Wuping died and was succeeded by his young son Zhou Baoquan; when Zhang Wenbiao of Hengzhou revolted, Zhou Baoquan asked Song for help. In 963 the Song army asked for passage through Jingnan, where Gao Jichong surrendered his lands; Zhang Wenbiao had meanwhile been put down by the Hunan general Yang Shifan, but the Song army entered Hunan all the same, defeated the Hunan fleet at Sanjiangkou, and Jinghu passed to the Song. Li Yu of Southern Tang (who succeeded in 961) followed the Song calendar, and Quanzhou and Zhangzhou were held by Chen Hongjin.

965.d: In the winter of Qiande 2 (964) Emperor Taizu of Song sent Wang Quanbin and Liu Guangyi against Shu by two routes; in the 1st month of 965 Meng Chang, ruler of Later Shu, surrendered, Later Shu fell, and Song gained forty-six prefectures. Southern Tang and Wuyue followed the Song calendar, while Northern Han still relied on Liao. Chen Hongjin of Quanzhou and Zhangzhou was invested as military governor of the Pinghai Jun. In Giao Châu the Ngô dynasty was in decline and fell into the division of the "Twelve Warlords". On the upper Yalu the remnants of the Balhae people founded the state of Jeongan.

971.d: In Qiande 6 (968) Đinh Bộ Lĩnh of Giao Châu put down the Twelve Warlords and founded the state of Đại Cồ Việt, with its capital at Hoa Lư. Emperor Taizu of Song attacked Taiyuan twice, in 968 and 969, failing both times because Liao came to its aid, and turned his campaigns south. In Kaibao 3 (970) Pan Mei invaded Southern Han and took Hezhou, Zhaozhou, Guizhou and Lianzhou in succession; in the 1st month of 971 he took Shaozhou, and in the 2nd month he entered Guangzhou; Liu Chang, the last ruler of Southern Han, surrendered, and Southern Han fell. In the same year Li Yu of Southern Tang gave up his state's name and styled himself "Ruler of Jiangnan", humbling himself still further before the Song.

975.d: In Kaibao 7 (974), on the pretext that Li Yu refused to come to court, Emperor Taizu of Song sent Cao Bin and Pan Mei against Southern Tang; the Song army crossed the Yangtze on a pontoon bridge at Caishiji, and in the 11th month of 975 took Jinling; Li Yu, the last ruler, surrendered, and Southern Tang fell. By now only Wuyue and the Chen family of Quanzhou and Zhangzhou remained in the south, and Northern Han and Liao in the north.

978.d: In Kaibao 9 (976) Emperor Taizu of Song died and his younger brother Zhao Guangyi took the throne (Emperor Taizong of Song). In the 4th month of Taiping Xingguo 3 (978) Chen Hongjin, military governor of Pinghai, handed over Zhangzhou and Quanzhou; in the 5th month Qian Chu, King of Wuyue, came to court and handed over the thirteen prefectures and one jun under his rule, "surrendering his lands to the Song". With that all the southern states had passed to the Song, leaving only Northern Han holding Taiyuan with Liao's help.

979.t: Song conquers Northern Han · Battle of the Gaoliang River
979.d: In 978 Chen Hongjin handed over Quanzhou and Zhangzhou, and Qian Chu, King of Wuyue, "surrendered his lands to the Song"; in 979 Emperor Taizong of Song led a campaign against Taiyuan in person, Liu Jiyuan of Northern Han surrendered, and the division of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms came to an end. Taizong pressed on to attack Liao, hoping to take Yan and Yun, but in the 7th month was badly beaten at the Gaoliang River outside Youzhou; the Song never recovered the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun. In the northwest the Tangut Dingnan Jun, the Guiyi Jun and the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom in Hexi, the Kingdom of Qocho (Uyghurs), the Kingdom of Khotan and the Kara-Khanid Khanate in the Western Regions, and in the southwest the Dali Kingdom and the Tibetan tribes, all lay outside the Song borders.
